clue.text: Start removing number of Romans from testudo in retreat

indicators.note: Removing a thing takes it out altogether, so the letter named next is struck from the word it sits in.
An army in retreat marches back the way it came, so the letters left over are read from the end to the start.

parts.note: the testudo was the tortoise formation Roman soldiers made with their shields
D is the Roman numeral for five hundred, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A legion giving up its shield formation and backing away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number of Romans' looks like a headcount of the legion and asks for one of their numerals instead. Six of the seven letters survive, and they read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The outset of a journey or a project is its start, the point everything is measured from.

clue.text: Outstanding secretary one had, inferior to Pierre's one

indicators.note: What is inferior to something sits below it, so in a downward answer the pieces named first are entered underneath the one that follows.

parts.note: Pierre is French, and one in French is un
a PA is a personal assistant, the secretary of an office
one is the figure 1, written as the letter I
had shrinks to the 'd of he'd and she'd

explanation.surface: A brilliant secretary ranked below a Frenchman of no distinction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is asked for twice in two languages, once as the French word and once as the figure. 'Outstanding' means remarkable in the surface and still-owed in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill left outstanding is one that has not been settled, so 'outstanding' and the answer both say the money never arrived.

clue.text: Litter in street and someone being sick

parts.note: St is street in any address
to retch is to heave as you are sick, so the person doing it is a retcher

explanation.surface: Rubbish dropped in the road beside somebody throwing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' is the crisp packets of the surface and the carrying frame of the answer, a word for it that survives mainly in sedan chairs and history books.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter is a frame for carrying a person lying down, which is exactly what ambulance crews carry the injured on.

clue.text: Try and listen to rap

definitions.meaning: the bug on a telephone line, where somebody is attempting to overhear a conversation that was not meant for them
the light knock on a door or a window pane

explanation.surface: Making an effort to get on with some modern music.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words run on as one sentence about music, so nothing marks the join after 'to' and the last word reads as the thing being listened to rather than a definition in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapping a phone is trying to listen to what is said on it, and tapping at a door is rapping on it.

clue.text: Computer confused the English hacker

indicators.note: Somebody confused has everything in the wrong order, so the words named come out in a new one.

parts.note: a Mac is Apple's computer
THE plus E for English, the four letters confused into a new order

explanation.surface: A muddled English computer expert breaking into a system.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface points at computing, and 'hacker' is the one that refuses to: this is the blade that hacks through undergrowth. E for English is the standard single letter, as in an E-numbered road sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is the broad-bladed knife used for hacking a way through cane or jungle, so it is a hacker in the literal chopping sense.

clue.text: Marriageable fellow failed to attend a ceremony, you hear

indicators.note: What you hear is the noise of the words rather than their spelling, so write down what the phrase named sounds like.

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony, and to miss one is to fail to attend it

explanation.surface: Somebody who never showed up at the service, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Said at speed, missed-a-rite and the answer are the same three noises, the 'a' doing the work of the unstressed syllable in the middle. The answer is what a hopeful romantic waits for.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Right is the man a woman is holding out to marry, so 'marriageable fellow' is the idiom stated plainly.

clue.text: Reliably hot region also coldest irregularly

indicators.note: Letters set down irregularly are not in their proper places, so the ones named are rebuilt in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A weather report claiming the same place is both the warmest and the chilliest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coldest' sits next to the definition's 'hot' so that the two cancel each other out in the reader's ear, and it is eight of the eleven letters. The region is the southern Spanish coast that package holidays sell for its sunshine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Costa del Sol is the stretch of Andalusian coast marketed on the dependability of its sun, which is what 'reliably hot region' says.

clue.text: Papers no longer like showing maidens inside

indicators.note: To show a thing is to let it be seen, and what the word before it shows is carried within its own letters.

parts.note: an ex-wife or ex-player is one no longer

indicators.note: What is put inside a thing sits within it, so the letter named goes into the middle of the word before it.

parts.note: swims like a fish is swims as a fish does
m is the column for maiden overs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: An old flame who is not as keen as she was on young women hanging about.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden over in cricket is one from which no runs are scored, and the scorebook writes it as a single m. 'Papers' is the pile the candidates sit rather than anything a journalist writes.
explanation.definitionFit: The papers a student sits are exams, the word standing for the question paper and the ordeal together.

clue.text: Service still no good

parts.note: even so and still are the same concession: it rained, still we went
n.g. is the old shorthand a marker writes for no good

explanation.surface: A tennis serve that was quiet and not up to much either.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' has to be read as a two-word phrase rather than the single adverb, which is where the clue hides its join. The service is the sung evening one in an Anglican church.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the evening service of the Church of England, so 'service' names the occasion it belongs to.

clue.text: What's needed to repair small cut on revolving belt?

indicators.note: Something revolving comes round to face the other way, so the word named is written from its end to its start.

parts.note: S is small on a clothes label
to pare an apple is to cut the peel away
a belt is a strap, here revolving to read the other way

explanation.surface: A small nick picked up from a moving fan belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolving belt' is the machine of the surface and a strap turned round in the wordplay, the same five letters either way. The question mark admits the definition is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare parts are the replacement components kept for a repair, so the phrase answers what a mechanic needs to put something right.

clue.text: Dictator's talented younger brother bumped off

indicators.note: A dictator is one who dictates, reading words out for somebody else to write, so what follows is spelt from the sound.

parts.note: somebody talented is able, and said aloud the two spellings cannot be told apart

explanation.surface: A tyrant's gifted little brother quietly got rid of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' is the strongman of the surface and the person reading a letter out in the wordplay. The definition is the first murder in Genesis, where Cain kills his younger brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel is the younger of Adam's two sons, killed by Cain, so the whole phrase names him by what happened to him.

clue.text: Crook did try and go for treatment

indicators.note: Anything sent for treatment comes back altered, so the letters named are rebuilt in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A patient who made an effort to turn up for the appointment.
explanation.walkthrough: The three little words carrying the letters are the sort a reader skates over, which is where the fodder hides. 'Crook' looks like the bent official of the surface and is precisely that.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirty dog is a scoundrel in the same breezy register as calling one a crook.

clue.text: Doctor's mother storing anything new in drawer

indicators.note: What a box is storing sits inside it, so the word named next goes within the letters before it.

parts.note: Dr is the doctor on a brass plate, and the possessive adds its s
aught is the old word for anything, as in for aught I know
ma is the informal mother
n is new in a dictionary or a catalogue

explanation.surface: A doctor's mother keeping every new thing she owns in a chest.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation swallows its own apostrophe-s, so Dr's is three letters before anything goes inside it. 'Drawer' is not furniture: it is somebody who draws, and the whole surface is arranged to stop you hearing it that way.
explanation.definitionFit: A draughtsman is a person who draws plans for a living, so 'drawer' names the job by the hand that does it.

clue.text: Help guitar player that's forgotten intro

indicators.note: A line that is forgotten never gets played, so the letter named is left out of the word it opens.

parts.note: the bassist is the one playing the bass guitar
the intro is the opening, so it is the first letter of the word, and it is the one dropped

explanation.surface: A band's guitarist coming in without playing the opening bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intro' does double service: it means the start of a track in the surface and the first letter of the word in the wordplay. The rest of the bassist is what is left standing.
explanation.definitionFit: To assist somebody is to help them, the verb in both cases.

clue.text: Try going viral — it's very upsetting

parts.note: a judge who tries a case is the judge who hears it
a post going viral is trending

explanation.surface: A court case that everybody online is suddenly sharing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like an attempt and is the courtroom sense, which is what puts the join in the middle of the first word rather than between the two. Both pieces are ordinary modern words and neither is abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heart-rending tears at you, which is upsetting at its strongest, and both are adjectives describing the thing that does it.

clue.text: Businessperson always with hot drink on the go?

definitions.text: Businessperson always with hot drink on the go?

parts.words: always with hot drink on the go?
parts.note: the reading the surface pushes: an executive who is never seen without a coffee in their hand
the reading the setter means: a trade in which the hot drink is the mash working away in the copper all day long

explanation.surface: An executive who is never caught without a coffee on the desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the go' turns between the two readings: in an office it means carried about, and in a trade it means in operation. The hot drink is spirit long before anyone would pour it.
explanation.definitionFit: A distiller's whole business is hot liquor running through a still from morning to night, so the description reads straight once 'drink' stops meaning something in a mug.

clue.text: Airborne swallows migrate

parts.note: a plane that is airborne is up
to swallow an insult is to stick it, both meaning to put up with it

explanation.surface: Swallows in flight heading off for the winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The birds are the trap: 'swallows' has to be read as the verb for putting up with something. To up sticks is to pull up your tent poles and move on.
explanation.definitionFit: To up sticks is to leave one home for another, which is what migrating is when people rather than birds do it.

clue.text: Removing these, does fat lady appear smaller?

definitions.text: Removing these, does fat lady appear smaller?

parts.note: read as dieting, this asks whether taking something off makes a woman look slimmer
the setter means putting the little binoculars down, after which the singer on the distant stage shrinks back to her real size

explanation.surface: A question about whether losing a few things would make somebody look thinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The fat lady is the operatic soprano of the proverb about when it is over, and the magnification is the only thing making her larger. Lower them and the stage goes back to being a long way off.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera glasses are the small binoculars taken to the theatre, and everything seen through them looks bigger, so removing them does shrink the singer.

clue.text: Statistical work, realm an actuary has covered

indicators.note: Something covered has another thing lying over it, so the letters wanted are buried under the words named.

parts.note: seven letters running on without a break across the three words

explanation.surface: An insurance man who has the whole kingdom's figures at his fingertips.
explanation.walkthrough: An actuary works out the odds on people dying for an insurer, so the surface holds together and hides the join. The word breaks fall in the middle of the letters wanted, which is what makes the run hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is the yearly book of tables and figures, tides and sunrises and averages, so 'statistical work' describes what is between its covers.

clue.text: Bags full of any number of nuts, bananas, crackers, etc

indicators.note: A bag full of something has it inside, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.

parts.note: sacks are the coarse bags potatoes come in
n stands for any number you like in algebra

explanation.surface: Sacks stuffed with an unspecified quantity of assorted madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts, bananas, crackers' is a list of three words for insane, and all three are also things you eat between meals. Reading them the second way is the whole solve.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts, bananas and crackers are all things eaten between meals, so the list defines by giving examples of the class.

clue.text: Fender includes one narrow part

indicators.note: A price that includes something has it within, so the letter named next sits inside the word before it.

parts.note: the Strat is Fender's Stratocaster, the guitar of a thousand rock records
one is the figure 1, written as the letter I

explanation.surface: A guitar model that comes with a slim component thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fender' reads as the bumper on a car and is the guitar firm, whose Stratocaster everybody shortens. The answer is a channel of sea, so it is a narrow part of water rather than of anything solid.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait is the narrow part of a sea between two larger stretches, as at Gibraltar or Dover.

clue.text: Heading north, graduate gripped compass

indicators.note: North is up the map, and a downward answer that goes up runs from its last letter to its first, so the word named is entered backwards.

parts.note: an MA is a graduate with a master's degree, here heading north up the column
a file that gripped the metal bit into it

explanation.surface: Somebody travelling up-country in the grasp of a university degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gripped' looks like the thing being done to the graduate and is a word in its own right, the past tense of bite. Compass here is the range a thing covers, as in the compass of a law.
explanation.definitionFit: The ambit of a rule or an inquiry is the extent of what it takes in, which is the sense 'compass' has outside navigation.

clue.text: Mint factory is keeping going

definitions.note: A mint is singular and the answer plural, but the idiom 'costs a mint' names an unspecified heap of money, which is the same thing the plural is doing.

parts.note: a mill is the factory a northern town grew around

indicators.note: Keeping something means holding on to it, so the word named next is held within the letters before it.

parts.note: the word itself, opened up to take another inside
a show that is going is on

explanation.surface: A mint still running as a factory after all these years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' is the place coins are struck in the surface, which is why the factory reads as scene-setting rather than as letters. A mint of money is an unspecified fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: To say something cost a mint is to say it cost millions, both being vague heaps of money rather than figures.

clue.text: Non-striker switched bats after changing ends in cricket

indicators.note: Two players who switched have each taken the other's place, so the four letters named come out back to front.
CRICKET opens on a c and closes on a t, and changing those two ends over puts the c where the t stands in the word beside it.

parts.note: the cricket bats of the surface, four letters with the third about to be traded

explanation.surface: A batsman at the bowler's end taking the strike once the pair have run.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the non-striker is the batter waiting at the far end, which is the sentence you read first; the answer is the other sort, the worker who keeps working while the union is out. 'Ends in cricket' points not at the pitch but at the outside letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A scab is somebody who crosses the picket line and carries on working, so 'non-striker' is the plain description of what a striking workforce is objecting to.

clue.text: Agency interested in aliens — one can blink strangely

indicators.note: Something done strangely is not done in the usual order, so the letters named are set down in another one.

parts.note: one is how a speaker refers to themselves, so it is me
eight more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A single alien proving it is capable of an odd sort of blink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is the formal pronoun for oneself, which is where the M and the E come from. The answer is the black-suited outfit of the films, so the definition names the agency by its business.
explanation.definitionFit: The Men in Black are the secret agency of the films whose entire job is aliens, and the name is what the public calls them.

clue.text: Tot your particular sequence of digits up

indicators.note: A downward answer read upwards runs from its foot to its top, so the letters named go in backwards.

parts.note: the number that is yours alone at a cash machine, taken from the top of the column downwards

explanation.surface: Adding up the digits of a number that belongs to you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digits' are fingers in one reading and the numerals of the answer in another, and 'tot' is a small measure of spirits rather than totting anything up.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot of whisky is a small measure poured, which is exactly what a nip is.

clue.text: In play, an act is very bad indeed

indicators.note: The play in a joint is the slack that lets it shift about, so the letters named do not stay where they were put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A single scene in a drama that is beyond redemption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In play' opens as the theatre of the surface and is the instruction, play being the looseness in a hinge. The definition is at its strongest: this is wickedness, not a poor performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Something satanic is evil of the devil's own kind, so the definition is the worst reading of 'bad' rather than the mildest.

clue.text: Neighbourhood what you'd expect, more or less

parts.note: par is the score expected on a golf hole, and below par is below what you expect
ish is the ending tacked on to a word to mean roughly, and it now stands alone

explanation.surface: Somebody reckoning that things have turned out about as predicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ish' as a word on its own is recent, spoken English, and it is doing all the work of 'more or less'. The answer is the area a church looks after, which is also how a village talks about its own patch.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish is the district round a church, used loosely for the neighbourhood everybody in it lives in.
